Styles / 38

Brutalist web design

A web style that deliberately looks raw and unadorned: near-default HTML with black text on white, blue underlined links, browser-default type and controls, and almost no decoration. Designers chose it from about 2014 as a reaction against polished, template-like sites. This record covers that raw core. The loud, chaotic branch that also uses the name is treated as antidesign.

Raw / Honest / Plain / Utilitarian / Contrarian

Visual grammar

  • HTML as material. The page shows its document structure: headings, paragraphs, bulleted lists, definition lists, and tables in their default form. Little or no layout grid.
  • Default type. Times or another browser-default serif for body text, sometimes a monospace throughout. Headings are bold and only one to two times the body size.
  • Black, white, and link blue. Pure black text on pure white. Links are the default blue (#0000EE) and underlined; visited links turn purple. Other color is rare and flat, often a single red for emphasis.
  • No polish. No shadows, gradients, or rounded corners. Borders come from default tables, inset rules, and gray push buttons.
  • Document flow. Content runs top to bottom at full width with the browser’s 8 px margin and default indents. Elements are not arranged into cards or columns.
  • Few images. Images, when present, sit inline at their natural size without frames, crops, or overlays.
  • No motion. No transitions or animation. Links and buttons give only the browser’s own feedback.

What connects the references

The core of the collection is written, not pictured. NN/g (2017) sets the scope: “bare-bones, almost naked HTML” with blue links and monospace text, and it puts the chaotic branch under antidesign. Smashing Magazine (2020) calls the same core l’Internet brut: light ground, black text, blue links. Copeland’s guidelines turn it into rules about behavior: underlined links, buttons that look like buttons, scrolling, and speed. His own site does not use default styles. Adobe (2016) dates the name and Deville’s motive, but its “more difficult to navigate” describes antidesign. NN/g (2025) separates plain-HTML brutalism from neobrutalism.

The look restates browser defaults. CSS 2 Appendix D and the WHATWG Rendering section document the 8 px body margin, h1 at 2em, h2 at 1.5em, underlined links, and the link colors #0000EE and #551A8B. The lineage records show where the defaults came from. The first website has black underlined links, a sans-serif heading, and no color. NCSA Mosaic brought blue links, on a gray ground. Both were plain because of their tools, not by choice.

Few references show the look directly. no style, please! is the clearest: black monospace on white, default blue and purple underlined links, nested default bullets, and no boxes, rules, or shadows. The Brutal WordPress theme keeps the small type scale (h1 at 1.5 times the body) but sets Roboto Mono and a 46em column. The Brutalist Pelican theme follows Copeland’s rules with Lato and dark gray links, which shows that the rules can travel without the look. Brutalist Websites itself is a short monospace text above a loose grid of screenshots.

The references disagree with the grammar on type and ground. The grammar and the specimen use Times, but no observed reference has serif body text: the directory, no style, please!, and the Brutal theme are monospace, NN/g describes monospace, and the first website is sans-serif. The serif rests only on the browser default. The directory uses a #eeeeee ground and the Mosaic record notes a gray ground, against the rule of pure white. The directory’s screenshot grid also breaks the diagnostic of one column of document flow.

Only the directory is measured, from a capture of 25 September 2026. It fails color.contrast: 18.1 against the minimum of 19.5, because of the gray ground. It passes type.sizeRange (1, one 13 px size throughout) and color.hues (1, link blue #0000ee), and it has no shadows, gradients, or radii. type.headingWeight reads null, because the page has no headings. Its color.imageShare of 0.36 is screenshots of other sites, which also add a red to the pixel palette. The specimen measures contrast 21, size range 2, and heading weight 700. The measurements cannot see whether plainness is chosen, so a 1990s page and a 2020 theme can measure the same. The fingerprint stays specimen-based until Copeland’s site and the Smashing examples, such as Craigslist and old Reddit, are captured.

Identity

Name
Name used by designers and vendors
Also called
Web brutalism, Brutalism (web design), l’Internet brut
Era
2014–present. Pascal Deville started brutalistwebsites.com in 2014. The look echoes 1990s websites such as Craigslist, which were plain because of early HTML and CSS, not by choice.
Regions
International
Name used by
Pascal Deville, Brutalist Websites (directory, from 2014), Kate Moran, Nielsen Norman Group, “Brutalism and Antidesign” (5 November 2017), Adobe Blog, “Brutalist Web Designers Eschew Rules for UX Best Practices” (1 December 2016), Smashing Magazine, “The Split Personality of Brutalist Web Development” (January 2020), David Bryant Copeland, “Guidelines for Brutalist Web Design” (updated 1 June 2025)

Lineage

  • Influenced by Brutalist architecture. The name and the idea of raw material come from architecture. NN/g (2017) and Copeland’s guidelines both cite béton brut and “truth to materials”. The link is by attitude, not by visual form.
  • Revival of Early web pages of the 1990s. NN/g (2017) says the style “echoes early 1990s-style websites (think Craigslist and the Drudge Report)”. Smashing Magazine (2020) calls the first website an “inadvertent disciple”.
  • Reaction against Flat design. Deville, quoted by Adobe (2016), describes a reaction to the “lightness, optimism, and frivolity” of web design shaped by Google and Apple. NN/g notes that both styles seek honesty by very different means.
  • Related to Neo-brutalism. Neo-brutalism of the 2020s took the name and the visible structure, then added bright fills, thick outlines, and hard shadows. The neo-brutalism record lists this style as its ancestor.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Links are blue and underlined, in the browser default color or close to it.
  • Body text is a default serif or monospace, black on white.
  • Headings are bold but small: at most about twice the body size.
  • Buttons, inputs, tables, and rules look like unstyled browser controls.
  • Content runs in one column of document flow, with no cards or decorative layout.

Rules it out

  • Shadows, gradients, rounded cards, or glass effects.
  • Bright fills on blocks, or thick black outlines with offset shadows (neo-brutalism).
  • Deliberate chaos: clashing colors, overlapping layers, odd cursors, or distracting animation (antidesign).
  • Carefully tuned type scale, custom typefaces, and generous designed whitespace.

Often confused with

Neo-brutalism
Neo-brutalism is a polished, colorful component system: thick black outlines, hard offset shadows, and bright flat fills. Brutalist web design has no fills or shadows and keeps browser-default controls.
Minimalist Machine
Minimalist Machine is designed: thin rules, outlined boxes, monospaced labels, and tuned spacing. Brutalist web design leaves styling at browser defaults, with serif body text and blue underlined links.
Antidesign
NN/g (2017) separates antidesign, which is often also called brutalism: harsh colors, no hierarchy, disorienting patterns and animation. Brutalist web design in this record is plain and readable, not chaotic.
Grunge typography
Grunge typography distresses and layers type for expression. Brutalist web design leaves type clean and default.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Write semantic HTML first and keep most elements at their browser-default look.
  • Use black text on white, a default serif or monospace, and blue underlined links. Let visited links turn purple.
  • Keep headings bold and small: h1 at about 2em, h2 at 1.5em.
  • Use native buttons, inputs, and tables with their default borders.
  • Put content in one column of document flow. Use rules and headings to separate sections.

Keep the function

  • Do not add shadows, gradients, rounded corners, or animation.
  • Do not turn content into cards, tiles, or hero banners.
  • Do not confuse raw with broken. Keep the page readable, keep links obvious, and keep the back button working.
  • Do not add clashing colors, overlapping layers, or odd cursors. That is antidesign, a different style.

Useful directions: personal sites and blogs, documentation and reference pages, classified listings and link directories, artist and designer portfolios that want an anti-polish stance, low-bandwidth or long-lived public information pages.

Poor fits:

  • Consumer brands that must feel warm, premium, or trustworthy to non-designers. The plain look can read as unfinished.
  • Rich applications such as dashboards and editors. Default controls do not scale to dense interaction.
  • Children's products and playful launches. The style is dry and austere.
